segments.quote: Where I'd now say it's thin is that it assesses the system as a camera system. It doesn't really assess it as a system that makes decisions about people in real time, because in 2022 the template I had didn't have a section for that.

codes.rationale: Officer openly critiques the limits of their own past assessment template and methodology.

segments.quote: It's a live document in the sense that the policy says it's a live document. Nobody has opened it since sign-off. There's no trigger — no review date, no event that causes someone to look at it again.

[Respondent] No. It's a live document in the sense that the policy says it's a live document. Nobody has opened it since sign-off. There's no trigger — no review date, no event that causes someone to look at it again. I could set one. I haven't.

codes.rationale: Absence of institutionalised review mechanisms means the evaluation trajectory is static.

segments.title: Questioning anonymity of derived counts
segments.quote: They are anonymous. They are also a complete record of how many people crossed which junction at what time for two years, and I'm not sure 'anonymous' is doing the work people think it's doing there.

[Respondent] Seventy-two hours for the raw video, indefinite for the derived counts. The derived counts are the interesting part and nobody asks about them because they're described as anonymous. codes.rationale: Critical scrutiny of assumptions regarding data anonymity and indefinite retention.

segments.title: Calibrating warnings too cautiously
segments.quote: I think the honest position is that I raise things in the strongest form I think will still get read, and I'm probably calibrating that too cautiously.
segments.full_text:
[Interviewer] Have you raised that?
[Respondent] In a footnote. I know how that sounds after what I just said about the risk register. I think the honest position is that I raise things in the strongest form I think will still get read, and I'm probably calibrating that too cautiously.

codes.rationale: Self-aware critique of internal communication strategies and self-censorship.

segments.title: Unexercisable subject access rights
segments.quote: So the right exists and is close to unexercisable. I've had two requests in two years and I couldn't fulfil either.
segments.full_text:
[Interviewer] Do residents have a route to see what data concerns them?
[Respondent] Subject access, in principle. In practice, to make a subject access request about camera footage you need to tell us approximately when and where you were, and most people can't, and the footage is gone in seventy-two hours anyway. So the right exists and is close to unexercisable. I've had two requests in two years and I couldn't fulfil either.

codes.rationale: Public participation and transparency rights are blocked by procedural and technical barriers.

summary: The respondent, a city council data protection officer, demonstrates strong epistemic reflexivity (P) by critically evaluating the shortcomings of past impact assessments, the limits of data anonymity, and their own cautious communication practices. However, the transcript reveals significant structural deficiencies across other dimensions. Anticipation (N) is undermined by static compliance templates that failed to foresee real-time decision-making systems. Responsiveness (N) is absent due to the lack of review triggers or mechanisms to adapt documentation over time. Finally, public engagement (N) is severely constrained because resident access rights are rendered practically unexercisable by short retention windows and excessive procedural demands. The multi-coded segment on the impact assessment effectively bridges reflexive self-critique with a retrospective account of failed anticipation.
transcript:
Interview transcript G06 — Data protection officer, city council
Case: Port Calder adaptive traffic signal and pedestrian detection system  |  SYNTHETIC DATA — not a real interview
[Interviewer] Was a data protection impact assessment done?
[Respondent] Yes, and it's a decent one, I'll defend it. It covers lawful basis, retention, access, the security arrangement, the processor terms. Where I'd now say it's thin is that it assesses the system as a camera system. It doesn't really assess it as a system that makes decisions about people in real time, because in 2022 the template I had didn't have a section for that.
[Interviewer] Has the assessment been revisited?
[Respondent] No. It's a live document in the sense that the policy says it's a live document. Nobody has opened it since sign-off. There's no trigger — no review date, no event that causes someone to look at it again. I could set one. I haven't.
[Interviewer] How is retention handled in practice?
[Respondent] Seventy-two hours for the raw video, indefinite for the derived counts. The derived counts are the interesting part and nobody asks about them because they're described as anonymous. They are anonymous. They are also a complete record of how many people crossed which junction at what time for two years, and I'm not sure 'anonymous' is doing the work people think it's doing there.
[Interviewer] Have you raised that?
[Respondent] In a footnote. I know how that sounds after what I just said about the risk register. I think the honest position is that I raise things in the strongest form I think will still get read, and I'm probably calibrating that too cautiously.
[Interviewer] Do residents have a route to see what data concerns them?
[Respondent] Subject access, in principle. In practice, to make a subject access request about camera footage you need to tell us approximately when and where you were, and most people can't, and the footage is gone in seventy-two hours anyway. So the right exists and is close to unexercisable. I've had two requests in two years and I couldn't fulfil either.
